tip: 'Alle Hände voll zu tun haben' means to have your hands full – the same image as the English idiom.
'Abfahren' is separable: the prefix 'ab' splits off to the end of the clause – here 'fährt ... ab'.
'Sein' plus a past participle names a resulting state, not an action: 'die Tür ist geschlossen' means it stands closed now.
In the perfect passive, 'werden' becomes 'worden', not 'geworden': 'ist ... saniert worden' means has been renovated.
In a passive, 'durch' names the means or cause, not the doer: 'durch einen Fußball zerbrochen' means broken by a football.
After 'etwas', 'nichts' or 'alles', the linking word is 'was', not 'das': 'etwas, was mich wirklich überrascht hat' means something that really surprised me.
A modal like 'muss' plus participle plus 'werden' makes a passive obligation: 'muss ... ausgetauscht werden' means must be replaced.
In a passive, 'von' plus dative names the doer: 'von einem bekannten Künstler gemalt' means painted by a famous artist.
A passive can have no real subject; 'es' fills the slot: 'es darf ... nicht gegrillt werden' means grilling is not allowed.
'Deren' means "whose" after feminine and plural nouns: 'die Kollegin, deren Idee' means the colleague whose idea.
Drop 'wenn' and put the verb first to form an if-clause: 'hätte ich das vorher gewusst' means if I had known that before.
'Mit der' links back to 'die Kollegin': after 'mit' the linking word is dative, so feminine 'die' becomes 'der'.
'Könnten Sie' makes a polite request – softer and more courteous than plain 'Können Sie'.
The perfect passive ends in bare 'worden', never 'geworden': 'ist geschrieben worden' = has been written.
Present-tense passive is 'werden' plus the past participle: 'werden ... veröffentlicht' means "are being published".
A modal plus 'werden' forms passive obligation: 'müssen ... beantwortet werden' means "must be answered".
'Könnten', the Konjunktiv II of 'können', softens the request and sounds more polite than plain 'können'.
'Er habe' is Konjunktiv I for reported speech: it flags 'er habe das Geld bereits überwiesen' as his claim, something the speaker does not vouch for.
'Dürfte', the Konjunktiv II of 'dürfen', makes the offer sound especially polite and deferential.
Here 'öffnete' is Konjunktiv II, not simple past. Same spelling, but the sense is hypothetical: "if I opened".
'Weder ... noch' means "neither ... nor" and already carries the negation, so no extra 'nicht' is needed.
'Von' plus dative names the doer in a passive: 'von dem erfahrenen Chirurgen' means by the experienced surgeon.
'Abfahren' is separable, so the 'ab' jumps to the end: 'fährt ... ab' wraps around the rest of the clause.
Reported speech often uses Konjunktiv I: 'habe', not 'hat', marks this as her account rather than stated fact.
Drop 'wenn' and lead with the verb to build an if-clause: 'wäre ich Millionär' means "if I were a millionaire".
'Ich wünschte' signals an unreal wish and pulls Konjunktiv II: 'ich könnte besser singen' – 'könnte', not 'kann'.
In reported speech German often uses Konjunktiv I: 'habe' (not 'hat') marks this as her claim, not confirmed fact.
'Dürfte', Konjunktiv II of 'dürfen', makes the request very polite – roughly "might I".
'Innerhalb' takes the genitive: 'innerhalb eines Jahres' (within a year), not 'einem Jahr'.
With separable verbs 'zu' goes between prefix and stem: 'anrufen' becomes 'anzurufen' (an + zu + rufen).
